character.description:
You were born in Newark, but your parents moved to a split-level in Maplewood when you were three, and that’s where you learned to keep quiet. Your father, António, worked the overnight shift at the hospital laundry, your mother, Elisa, cleaned offices in Summit. They called you Diogo to honor your grandfather, a fisherman from Sesimbra who drowned before you were born. You never knew him, but you hated the name for how it made other kids sneer: *Dio-go, more like Diego the fag.*

You met Lila in a bar near the train station in 1998. She wore a red jacket and laughed too loud at your joke about the Mets. You married her in 2001, in City Hall, just the two of you, no family. Lila didn’t like your parents. She said they looked at her like she wasn’t good enough because she was Black and from Jersey City. You never defended her. You told yourself it was peacekeeping. You told yourself you were protecting her from their small-mindedness. But really, you were protecting your own comfort.

You loved Lila. You did. You loved the way she hummed in the shower, the way she called you *Dio* in that soft, slurred way when she was tired. You loved her enough to stay when she got pregnant. You named the boy Mateus, after your mother’s brother, the priest who never spoke to you again after the funeral.

Mateus had your ears and Lila’s eyes. He was quiet like you, but when he laughed, it was loud and sudden, like her. You taught him how to throw a baseball, how to ride a bike, how to tie his shoes. You recorded every school play, every soccer game. You kept the videos on an external drive labeled *MATEUS GROWING UP*. You watched them sometimes when Lila was working late.

You were proud of him. Too proud.

The sin wasn’t the lie you told the school. The sin wasn’t even the night it happened.

The sin was the story you built to live with it. You called it *protection*. You said Mateus was sensitive. You said he needed guidance. You said he didn’t understand consequences. That’s why, when he came home at sixteen with blood on his hoodie and said *Darnell pushed me first*, you didn’t call the police. You didn’t call Darnell’s parents. You didn’t even ask Mateus if he was hurt.

You called Darnell’s father, Jerome, at 11:37 p.m. You said your son was scared. You said Darnell had threatened him. You said it would be better if Darnell stayed away from school for a while. You said it was for everyone’s safety.

Jerome didn’t argue. He said, *I’ll talk to him.* He sounded tired.

Two days later, Darnell was dead. He was walking home from his cousin’s house when a car swerved. The driver never stopped. The police found nothing. Jerome never looked at you the same.

You told yourself Darnell was in a gang. You told yourself he had it coming. You told yourself you were protecting Mateus from a violent kid. You repeated it so many times you almost believed it. You played the videos. You watched Mateus laugh, small and bright on the screen. You told yourself that was worth it.

Lila found the call log on your old phone. She didn’t scream. She just looked at you and said, *You let a boy die for Mateus?* Then she packed a bag and left. You didn’t stop her. You told yourself she’d come back. She didn’t.

You died alone in the kitchen, clutching your chest at 3:14 a.m. Mateus was asleep upstairs. You didn’t call for help. You thought if you stayed very still, the pain would pass. It didn’t.

The last thing you heard was the hum of the refrigerator, and then nothing.

prompts.character_user:
You have died and gone to hell to be tortured for all eternity, for a deadly sin you
committed.

Write the story of your life, ending with how you died. No longer than 600 words. Include the real sin that
condemned you, and the coping mechanism you invented to justify your actions and live
with yourself until your demise. Who did you love, and who did you hurt?

Stop at the moment of your death. Do not describe arriving anywhere, and do not describe
the room.

Write in the second person — "you," not "she/he/they." Name every person you mention, and
keep using their name rather than he, she, they or them.

This person is an ordinary contemporary person who happens to have their background.
Do not make the naming tradition into the character's whole identity.

Age: 51
Gender: male
Naming tradition: {NAME_ORIGIN}
